query: Reported superconducting high-entropy alloys are dominated by Nb-Ta matrices, while other studies concern titanium-rich systems based on heavy transition metals and partly ordered systems. Consequently, these precedents do not establish what controls superconductivity in high-entropy alloys outside the best-studied material classes. Within the defining constraint of a solid solution containing at least five elements at no less than 5 atomic percent each, what governs superconducting behavior in such an uncharacterized high-entropy alloy, and why? State one testable mechanistic hypothesis, a controlled comparison against the starting material, predicted observations relative to the baseline, applicable boundary conditions, the earlier evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy alloys outside the well‐studied Nb–Ta or Ti‐rich systems, superconductivity is primarily governed by the magnitude of local lattice distortions induced by atomic size mismatches. These distortions modulate the density of states at the Fermi level and the electron–phonon coupling strength, thereby controlling the superconducting transition temperature.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase, disordered solid-solution HEA (with a minimum of five elements each at no less than 5 atomic percent) exhibiting a typical BCC or FCC structure.
generation.intervention: Reduce the overall atomic size disparity by substituting one or more elements with alternatives of similar atomic radii (while keeping the compositional complexity) to systematically lower local lattice distortions.
generation.conditions: Low-temperature measurements under identical processing and synthesis conditions that preserve the single-phase disordered state; comparisons are to be made with the original HEA baseline.
generation.structural_mediator: The local lattice distortions/microstrain, which can be quantified by X-ray diffraction line broadening or extended X-ray absorption fine structure (EXAFS) analyses.
generation.mechanism: A reduction in atomic size mismatch decreases local lattice distortion, leading to a more sharply defined electronic density of states at the Fermi level. This change enhances electron–phonon coupling, resulting in a higher superconducting transition temperature (Tc) and a sharper superconducting transition.
generation.predicted_outcome: The modified HEA with reduced atomic size disparity will exhibit a higher Tc and a narrower superconducting transition compared to the baseline alloy with larger atomic mismatches.
generation.baseline: The original HEA, featuring a larger degree of atomic size mismatch and associated lattice distortions, which is expected to show a lower Tc and a broader superconducting transition.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies as long as the alloy remains a single-phase disordered solid solution; if the compositional changes induce phase separation or ordering, the governing mechanism for superconductivity may differ.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative change in Tc is uncertain given the complex interplay of disorder and electron scattering in HEAs. Further experimental studies are needed to determine the exact magnitude of the effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of HEA samples under identical conditions: one set as the baseline alloy with a relatively high atomic size disparity and a second set with targeted elemental substitutions that reduce atomic size mismatches. Ensure both sets remain as single-phase disordered solid solutions. Measure and compare their superconducting transition behaviors using resistivity (four-probe measurements) and magnetic susceptibility tests.
measurements: Critical superconducting temperature (Tc) from resistivity vs temperature curves
Transition sharpness (i.e., width of the superconducting transition)
Characterization of lattice distortions via XRD (peak broadening) or EXAFS
Density of states near the Fermi level via tunneling spectroscopy, if available
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA with reduced atomic size mismatch does not exhibit a statistically significant increase in Tc (or a notably sharper superconducting transition) relative to the baseline alloy, the hypothesis that local lattice distortions from atomic size mismatches govern the superconducting behavior will be falsified.
